title: Why lab data matters in the CMS ACCESS model
summary: Electronic health records integrations with genetic testing increases operational efficiency, enhances the provider experience and offers precision medicine at scale.
body_markdown:
As value-based care continues to evolve, organizations face growing pressure to demonstrate measurable improvements in patient health instead of documenting delivery of services. The new[CMS ACCESS](https://www.cms.gov/priorities/innovation/innovation-models/access) (Advancing Chronic Care with Effective, Scalable Solutions) Model reflects that shift with a straightforward premise: Chronic disease management in Medicare hasn't kept pace with what patients actually need.


ACCESS is creating a framework rewarding organizations for helping patients achieve meaningful health outcomes through technology-enabled chronic care support rather than traditional fee-for-service activities. The result is a 10-year alternative payment model that shifts how technology-supported care is delivered and reimbursed, built around a question that value-based care leaders have been asking for years: What if payment were tied to whether patients actually get better?


While much of the discussion surrounding ACCESS has focused on digital health platforms, remote monitoring, and virtual care, another component sits at the center of outcome measurement: objective clinical data. Lab testing plays an important role throughout the patient journey, helping clinicians:


- Establish baselines
- Monitor disease progression
- Evaluate treatment effectiveness
- Measure clinical improvement over time


For provider organizations, ACOs, CINs, and health systems weighing what ACCESS participation means in practice, a large part depends on the quality of clinical data supporting care decisions every step of the way.


## What is the ACCESS Model?


ACCESS is a voluntary CMS Innovation Center model designed to expand access to technology-supported chronic disease management for people with Original Medicare. It targets conditions affecting more than[two-thirds of Medicare beneficiaries](https://www.cms.gov/priorities/innovation/access-primary-care-providers-referring-clinicians) , including:


- Anxiety
- Diabetes
- Depression
- High blood pressure
- Chronic musculoskeletal pain
- Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
- Cardio-kidney-metabolic conditions such as chronic kidney disease


The model is voluntary and complements, rather than replaces, the role of primary care providers (PCPs) and referring clinicians. Participating organizations share structured care updates throughout the patient experience from the start of care, during escalations, and at care completion to help maintain continuity and support informed clinical decision-making.


Referring clinicians who review those updates and document coordination activity can bill a co-management payment. It's an integrated framework, not a parallel system leaving PCPs out of the loop.


Under ACCESS, participating organizations provide technology-enabled care services that may include:


- Remote monitoring
- Patient education
- Lifestyle coaching
- Behavioral support
- Care coordination
- Medication management


CMS established the model to give patients additional options for managing chronic conditions between office visits while making sure care remains coordinated with PCPs and referring clinicians.


## Why CMS created ACCESS OR How ACCESS differs from traditional chronic care management


Traditional chronic care management programs have always faced a structural tension: They pay for touchpoints, not trajectories. A care coordinator call, a patient education session, a remote monitoring subscription all generate a reimbursable event.


Outcomes such as a patient's HbA1c, blood pressure target, or LDL cholesterol were tracked for quality reporting but rarely drove the payment calculation directly. ACCESS changes that relationship fundamentally.


Technology-enabled care is the delivery mechanism, not the product. The product is a measurable improvement in patient health, and the clinical evidence that demonstrates that comes from objective biomarkers:


- Weight measurements
- HbA1c levels
- Blood pressure readings
- Urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR)
- Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
- Lipid panels to measure cholesterol


Patient-reported outcome measures capture pain, mood, and functional status alongside those biomarkers to provide a fuller picture. Without consistent clinical measurement, it becomes difficult to understand whether a patient's health status has changed, whether an intervention is working, or whether additional treatment adjustments may be necessary.


The ACCESS Model introduces outcome-aligned payments, which tie reimbursement to measurable patient outcomes rather than a defined set of activities. Participating organizations receive recurring payments for managing qualifying chronic conditions, with full payment linked to achieving clinical improvement against established outcome targets.


Many technology-enabled chronic care programs deliver their value through ongoing engagement, continuous monitoring, and long-term behavior changes that don’t exactly fit into conventional billing models, yet allow them to fit neatly into the ACCESS Model.


CMS organized these into clinical tracks, each with condition-specific measures and outcome targets informed by clinical guidelines. Payment depends on the share of an organization's patients who meet those targets compared against a minimum threshold that rises each participation year.


## Why ACCESS isn’t just a digital health conversation


The ACCESS Model isn't primarily a digital health program, even though technology-supported care is central to it. Digital tools facilitate care delivery, but they don't generate the clinical evidence that satisfies an outcome target on their own.


A wearable device may collect activity data. A coaching platform may encourage healthier behaviors. A remote care team may provide education and support. However, a validated HbA1c result is what tells a clinician and CMS whether the intervention is working.


That distinction has significant implications. Technology-enabled care can facilitate communication, encourage adherence, and extend clinical support beyond the clinic. Yet technology alone can’t demonstrate improved health outcomes.


Organizations must also document objective evidence that patients are making measurable progress. This is where clinical and laboratory data become especially important.


## Where lab data supports patient success


By July 2027, all ACCESS organizations must connect to a CMS Aligned Network or Health Information Exchange, making structured patient data that includes biomarkers, patient-reported outcomes, and medications searchable through existing EHR workflows. That infrastructure integration matters because consistent, standardized lab data is what transforms a care coordination record into a longitudinal clinical picture.


Here are four reasons why:


**1. It helps establish a baseline**


Before improvement can be measured, clinicians need an accurate picture of a patient's current health status. Biomarkers such as HbA1c, LDL cholesterol, kidney function markers, and other lab results provide quantitative benchmarks against which future progress can be assessed.


**2. It helps identify risk and stratify patient populations**


Chronic disease management programs often focus resources on patients who are most likely to benefit from additional intervention. Clinical lab data can help uncover uncontrolled disease, worsening trends, or emerging complications that may otherwise go unnoticed.


**3. It allows for longitudinal monitoring**


Chronic conditions evolve over months and years. Reliable lab data helps care teams track disease progression and evaluate response to treatment, lifestyle modifications, medication adjustments, or technology-supported interventions.


An HbA1c drawn at enrollment isn't meaningful in isolation, but it becomes meaningful when it's comparable to the next result, and the one after that, across a patient population with heterogeneous risk profiles and comorbidities.


A remote monitoring notification tells a care team that something may have changed. A lab result tells them what changed and by how much.


That distinction can also help organizations assess the effectiveness of care programs. While engagement metrics may show that patients are participating in remote monitoring, coaching, or care management programs, longitudinal clinical data provides objective evidence of whether those interventions are influencing outcomes.


In a model where reimbursement is increasingly tied to measurable improvement, this visibility helps organizations understand not only clinical performance, but the value generated by their technology-enabled care investments.


**4. It helps demonstrate outcomes**


If the goal is to improve diabetes control, lower cardiovascular risk, or slow kidney disease progression, lab biomarkers provide objective evidence of change. That evidence supports both clinical decision-making and performance measurement within value-based care frameworks.


Lab testing isn’t the sole driver of outcomes. Successful chronic disease management also depends on:


- Care coordination
- Patient engagement
- Behavioral support
- Medication adherence
- Clinician oversight


However, lab data provides an essential measurement framework for evaluating whether those efforts translate into meaningful clinical improvement. The organizations that perform well under ACCESS will be the ones reliably tracking those trajectories, identifying patients who aren't responding to interventions early enough to adjust, and demonstrating aggregate outcome improvement across their enrolled population at the end of a payment period.


## Practical implications for organizations exploring ACCESS participation


The ACCESS Model reflects a broader transformation occurring across healthcare. Payment increasingly aligns with measurable outcomes, care extends beyond traditional clinical settings, and organizations need greater visibility into patient progress between visits.


As you evaluate whether or not and how to participate in ACCESS, data infrastructure deserves the same attention as care delivery workflows. The clinical tracks with the highest biomarker-driven outcome targets, particularly the cardio-kidney-metabolic track, will reward organizations that can maintain consistent testing cadences and act on results in near real time.


As organizations expand technology-enabled care capabilities, the ability to integrate longitudinal clinical data becomes increasingly important. Fragmented information can limit visibility into patient progress, complicate care coordination, and make it harder to assess program effectiveness.


The challenge is no longer simply obtaining lab results. It's creating a consistent view of patient progress across populations and care settings. Labcorp's scale and standardized data infrastructure are designed to help support that visibility.


Our longitudinal, standardized data platform helps organizations move beyond individual test results to understand patient and population health trends over time. With more than 45 billion test results, approximately 160 million patient encounters annually, and lab data representing roughly half of the U.S. population, Labcorp provides the scale and continuity needed to support risk identification, care gap management, outcome measurement, and value-based care initiatives.


With ACCESS, the ability to connect technology-enabled care with objective clinical evidence will become increasingly important. Our[lab data and analytics capabilities](https://www.labcorp.com/data) can help provide the longitudinal visibility needed to measure progress, assess program effectiveness, and support outcome-focused care delivery.


With these capabilities, organizations can gain a more comprehensive view of patient health over time and better understand patterns of disease progression and improvement.


As payment models become increasingly outcome-focused, organizations face growing pressure to demonstrate that technology-enabled care programs are producing measurable clinical results. The ability to connect patient engagement efforts with objective evidence of improvement can help healthcare leaders evaluate program performance, identify opportunities for earlier intervention, and better understand the return on investments in chronic disease management.


## The value-based care challenge: Data without direction


Diagnostics—sometimes viewed as a transactional lab service—can be a powerful upstream driver of value-based care success with the right strategic partner. One reason provider organizations and health plans struggle to turn clinical data into strategic action to improve outcomes and equity is the limited coordination, fragmented systems and/or separate data workflows between providers and labs, resulting in impeding effective use of diagnostic data.


When integrated into care management workflows, diagnostic data can help improve coding accuracy, real-time risk stratification and targeted interventions to ensure the right care at the right time and close gaps in care, while also expanding access and advancing health equity.


## Three ways to use diagnostics as a strategic asset


Diagnostic data has a strategic value that goes far beyond test results. In addition to its ROI and effect on CMS Stars and HEDIS reporting, it can provide visibility into longitudinal patient data such as lab results ordered by providers outside of the network, helping target care gaps associated with payer quality incentives. When integrated into workflows, lab data becomes a catalyst for:


**1. Earlier detection, improved risk identification, stratification and coding accuracy**


Using comprehensive laboratory data from diverse sources, organizations can create a more complete patient risk profile, and gain early, valuable insights into patient health status, risk factors and potential disease progression. This information assists providers in proactively implementing prioritized and[tailored interventions](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/applying-lab-data-combat-chronic-conditions-strategic-gaps-care-approach) for patients who need it the most, ultimately improving outcomes and reducing healthcare costs.


Lab data can also help organizations identify uncoded or misdiagnosed chronic conditions—especially in new patient panels. For example:


- 20%-30% of diabetic patients go uncoded
- 70% of chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients are either uncoded and/or aren’t accurately coded for the appropriate stage


Organizations that align lab results with existing patient coding can support appropriate risk adjustment and anticipate future care needs. This enables early detection of high-risk patients, more accurate prediction of disease progression, accurate payment based on the risk of the population and better allocation of care management resources.


Labcorp’s national lab data and[Insight Analytics®](https://www.labcorp.com/data/insight-analytics) platform help providers reconcile coding discrepancies, align documentation with actual patient health status and prepare for the transition to the V28 HCC coding model. In fact, we helped one large provider network[uncover a potential $14 million annual impact](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/how-lab-data-enables-more-accurate-patient-coding-value-based-care-success) by correcting coding for diabetes and CKD.


**2. Solving for silos and fragmented systems with seamless integration into care management workflows**


Effective integration of diagnostic data into care management workflows is at the heart of successful value-based care initiatives and crucial for improving patient outcomes. However, siloed data and fragmented workflows can hinder care coordination and impede progress.


Organizations that seamlessly integrate diagnostic data into care management workflows can streamline processes, enhance communication and make sure critical information is readily available to all stakeholders. It helps providers make informed decisions, facilitate timely interventions and foster collaboration among care teams, ultimately leading to improved patient experiences and better health outcomes.


Integrating solutions that feed data analytics platforms into provider workflows also provides[comprehensive lab utilization](https://www2.labcorp.com/three-lab-stewardship-utilization-rights-underutilization-focus) , results values and related patient data that reduces patient and provider friction and improves efficiency.


Seamlessly integrating data into care management workflows helps:


- Assess disease prevalence
- Support planning for access and well-being across populations
- Optimize provider test ordering and utilization
- Support clinical decision-making at the point of care
- Streamline result delivery and eliminate manual data entry
- Gain real-time access to lab histories, regardless of ordering provider
- More effectively close gaps in care


Labcorp’s tools, including[Diagnostic Assistant®](https://www.labcorp.com/data/diagnostic-assistant) , break down lab data siloes and embed them into the care continuum—supporting timely interventions, accurate documentation and coordinated care. The Insight Analytics dashboards also offer predefined population health analysis, allowing administrators to quickly identify patients with multiple overdue tests. Shared access to lab results, outcomes and cost data align providers, payers and care teams around a single source of truth, improving clinical decision-making.


**3. Advancing health outcomes across populations through access and outreach**


Ensuring access and well-being across populations is a fundamental pillar of value-based care and diagnostic services play a pivotal role in addressing disparities in access to preventive care. Health equity gaps lead to missed opportunities for early intervention, preventing disease progression and providing more cost-effective care.


Health equity isn’t just about ensuring access and well-being for all—it also can be a key performance driver. Yet:


- Over[100 million Americans face barriers](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/health/2023/02/28/americans-lack-primary-care-provider-report/11359096002/) to primary care
- One in three Americans experiences[at least one care gap](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5348227/)
- 50% of adults[skip routine screenings,](https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/payers/half-us-adults-avoid-health-screenings-survey-finds) and along with chronic diseases and mental health conditions,[drive $4.1 trillion](https://www.cdc.gov/pcd/issues/2024/23_0267.htm#:~:text=Besides%20the%20personal%20impact%2C%20chronic,mental%20health%20conditions%20(6).) in annual healthcare costs


Lab diagnostics can play a significant role in promoting access and well-being across populations by identifying and addressing disparities in healthcare outcomes. Integrated, innovative solutions can help organizations understand[health trends in specific geographies](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/leveraging-lab-data-combat-diabetes-and-chronic-kidney-disease) and socially vulnerable patient populations.


Providers can use these insights to make data-driven decisions for targeted, personalized interventions to more effectively address gaps in care. Labcorp has lab data on over 50% of the U.S. population, helping you identify and address care gaps with patient-centric solutions, including:


- Access to over 2,200 patient service centers and their partnerships with Walgreens that expand local access
- Multilingual outreach and culturally tailored engagement to improve compliance among diverse populations
- Access to community-based lab data for disease trending, benchmarking and identifying underserved populations
- Health equity dashboards that combine geo-coded disease prevalence with area deprivation indices to help target interventions
- At-home testing **** kits to expand access and reach patients where they’are, reducing geographic and logistical barriers, especially for underserved populations
- An Open Orders program that sends personalized email reminders to patients, resulting in improved patient compliance and supporting quality measure performance
- The ability to generate actionable lists for care coordination teams to engage patients and address health concerns and target patients with overdue testing


By pairing member education that highlights the importance of routine medical care with convenient and accessible diagnostic services, healthcare organizations can improve coordination across the care continuum and provide actionable information to connect members with the next steps in their healthcare journey.
